title: The Discipline Required To Create The Life You Want
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Ryan Holiday argues against the reflexive impulse to scale everything, using his own decision to run a single small bookstore in rural Texas—rather than expand it or chase a bigger venture—as the frame. He draws on Nate Silver's observation that the venture-capital "obsession with scale" has wrongly become the default success metric for creative and media work that would be better modeled on running one great restaurant. The essay's spine is a line from The 48 Laws of Power, "Do Not Go Past The Mark You Aimed For," which Holiday uses to argue that discipline means defining what winning looks like and stopping there rather than chasing indiscriminate growth. He applies this to his own choices—writing about Stoicism rather than more commercial genres, declining to turn The Daily Stoic into a merch or licensing empire—and reframes the goal of a working life as protecting an "ideal ordinary day" rather than deferring happiness to some future payoff. The piece closes as a list of specific disciplines: to know what you want, to turn down lucrative opportunities, and to say no to those pushing expansion. It fits Leadership for its argument about professional character, decision-making, and resisting external pressure to conform to a conventional definition of success.
points: Uses his own decision to open a small bookstore in rural Texas—rather than scale a tech or investing venture—as the entry point for an argument against indiscriminate growth.
Cites Nate Silver's "obsession with scale" framing: the venture-capital mindset wrongly applied to creative and media careers that would be better modeled on running one great restaurant.
Invokes the 48 Laws of Power principle "Do Not Go Past The Mark You Aimed For" as the discipline of knowing when you've won and stopping there.
Argues most people chase growth indiscriminately because they never define what success or "enough" actually looks like for themselves.
Frames declining lucrative opportunities (a D.C. job, startup investing, brand licensing) as evidence of protecting an "ideal ordinary day" rather than deferring life to a future payoff.
quotes: I was the crazy one who decided to open a small bookstore in rural Texas.
What strikes me isn't that people ask—it's how instinctively they ask. As if expansion were the only logical next step.
Do Not Go Past The Mark You Aimed For" is one of the most important laws in The 48 Laws of Power.
So many people think they have to live a life they don't want for a long time so that eventually, off in the distant future, they can live a life they do want.
I've always found it's better to think about what my ideal ordinary day looks like. That, at least, is the mark I am aiming for: for that ideal ordinary day to be most of my days.
